title: SYSK Selects: How Traffic Works
summary: A Saturday "SYSK Selects" rerun of the 2010 episode "How Traffic Works." Chuck introduces it, then Josh and Chuck discuss the two causes of traffic (congestion and unpredictable incidents), traffic waves and Josh's "traffic bubble" analogy, the costs of traffic, the Texas Transportation Institute's travel time index, Atlanta and Los Angeles traffic, latent demand from highway widening, ramp metering (Minnesota study), HOV lanes, congestion pricing (London, Singapore, Stockholm, UK debate), traffic light timing, passenger car equivalents, and a "virtual slots" idea. The episode closes with listener Facebook questions on unusual foods, the tree-falling-in-forest question, where former hosts are now, Athens bars, celebrity fans, and pirates as ninjas.

segments.title: Selects intro
segments.summary: Chuck introduces the SYSK Selects weekend repost of the July 2010 episode How Traffic Works.

segments.title: Opening banter
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck trade off-topic banter about public transit, sunglasses, and past spoilers before starting the traffic discussion.

segments.title: Causes of traffic and traffic waves
segments.summary: Traffic arises from congestion or unpredictable incidents such as breakdowns, wrecks, or police pullovers. A single braking event propagates backward as a traffic wave. Josh describes his 'traffic bubble' analogy for how braking slows cars behind until the wave passes.

segments.title: Costs of traffic
segments.summary: Estimated traffic costs of about seventy-eight billion dollars a year covering fuel and wasted time, excluding pollution and health costs. Extra gasoline in 2007 and per-motorist cost figures are cited, along with Commute Solutions' estimate of per-mile driving cost.

segments.title: Travel time index and city rankings
segments.summary: The Texas Transportation Institute's travel time index compares rush-hour travel time to off-peak travel time within the same city. Los Angeles and Atlanta are discussed as among the worst cities, with Boston, Seattle, San Francisco and Washington D.C. also mentioned.

segments.title: Driving habits and highway speeds
segments.summary: Anecdotes about California Highway Patrol pace cars and Atlanta drivers routinely going about seventy miles an hour. Surface streets, not just highways, are discussed as carrying overflow traffic.

segments.title: Latent demand and highway widening
segments.summary: Half of car travel occurs on highways, though they are a small share of roads. Widening highways creates latent demand that fills new lanes, so it does not reduce congestion. Light rail is suggested as an alternative.

segments.title: Ramp metering and HOV lanes
segments.summary: Ramp meters allow one car through every few seconds at highway on-ramps. A Minnesota study found traffic accidents rose when meters were shut off for seven weeks and capacity rose fourteen percent when they were restored. HOV or carpool lanes are discussed, with complaints about solo drivers using them.

segments.title: Congestion pricing
segments.summary: Road pricing, which charges drivers to enter congested areas, is discussed. London, Singapore, Stockholm and a pilot program are mentioned. The UK debate over national road pricing under Lord Adonis and Alistair Darling is covered, along with equity concerns that peak-hour pricing burdens workers who cannot be flexible.

segments.title: Traffic lights, suburban sprawl and vehicle size
segments.summary: Poorly timed traffic lights are criticized, with comparison of timed and sensor-based signals and citywide coordinated plans. Suburban sprawl adding cars to roads not built for them is noted. Passenger car equivalents rate SUVs and city buses as heavier in traffic, and virtual slots are proposed as a theoretical fix.

segments.title: Listener questions and outro
segments.summary: Facebook questions covering unusual foods, the tree-falling-in-the-forest question, where former co-hosts are now, Athens bars, celebrity fans, and the term for pirates. Contact information and website plug close the episode.
